documents.title: Call from patient's mother
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Mother called, patient on the line and gave verbal permission for me to talk with both of them. Mother reports Paige has been pulling away for about two years: stays in her room, has been heard talking to herself, and has said things the family finds strange about the TV news and about her professors. Paige was guarded on the phone, said she is "just tired" and that people at school are not being straight with her. Would not say more. Asked directly: she said she sometimes thinks about not being here but has no plan and has not done anything to hurt herself. Mother staying with her this week.

This needs a psychiatric evaluation soon. Paige agreed. Urgent referral to outpatient psychiatry placed; family will drive her. Gave both of them the crisis line and told them to go to the ED for any thoughts of acting on it. I'd like to see her in the office after she's been evaluated.

procedures.procedure: Psychiatric diagnostic evaluation with medical services

documents.title: Outpatient Psychiatry Initial Evaluation
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
OUTSIDE PSYCHIATRY GROUP
Initial psychiatric evaluation, 5/27/2022
Re: Paige Howland, DOB 6/28/1995
Referred by: primary care

Reason for evaluation: 26-year-old graduate student brought in by her parents, who describe roughly two years of withdrawal, talking under her breath when alone, and increasingly unusual beliefs.

History: Per parents, she spends most of the day in her room. Paige herself describes a conviction that television news presenters are directing concealed messages at her, and that faculty in her department are taking her research ideas by way of "electromagnetic readings." She reports voices that remark on what she is doing, heard when no one else is present. Mood: she describes stretches of feeling "numb" lasting weeks, with so little energy she skips showering and meals. Frequently hopeless. Has passing thoughts about death; no intent, plan or preparatory acts. Denies any period of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep or impulsive behavior.

Past psychiatric history: a depressive episode in college (2016), counseling only. Last year, a depressive episode of about three months in which the same voices and suspiciousness were present. Records reviewed show an inpatient psychiatric stay approximately six months ago at another hospital for auditory hallucinations and delusional thinking; at that time she reported no depressive or manic symptoms. She cannot recall being sent home on any medication, and the discharge paperwork was not available to us.

Medical: none. Surgical: none. Medications: none. Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: mother with major depression; maternal aunt with bipolar disorder; maternal uncle with schizophrenia.
Social: graduate student, lives with a roommate. No alcohol, tobacco or drugs.

Mental status: appropriately dressed, cooperative, eye contact minimal. Speech at times tangential and hard to follow. Mood "flat." Affect constricted. Thought content with referential and persecutory delusions as above. Endorses auditory hallucinations. Passive death wish without intent or plan. Insight limited, judgment fair.

Physical exam: within normal limits. Screening labs today (CBC, BMP, TSH) unremarkable.

Formulation: psychotic symptoms present for more than two weeks without mood symptoms (the inpatient episode), alongside recurrent major depressive episodes with psychosis, now again depressed with psychosis.
Diagnosis: Schizoaffective disorder, depressive type.

Risk: chronic elevated risk given diagnosis and hopelessness; acute risk judged low today (no intent or plan, family support, future oriented about her degree). Safety plan completed with her and parents.

Plan:
1. Weekly individual psychotherapy, referral given.
2. Medication options discussed at length. She prefers to hold off for now and start with therapy; we will revisit at each visit.
3. Return in 3 months, sooner as needed. Crisis numbers provided.

Copy to primary care.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen after her psychiatry evaluation; their letter is in the chart. She came alone. She learned there that she was hospitalized last fall at another hospital; she had not told us and we never got records. Says she has been to two therapy sessions and likes the therapist. Not on medication, her choice for now, and psychiatry is following.

She describes low energy and not eating much. Down about 1.5 kg since 2019. Still hears a voice now and then, less when she's busy. Passive thoughts of death on bad days, no intent, no plan, no access to firearms. Parents check in daily.

Exam: thin, quiet, fair grooming. Vitals fine. Heart and lungs normal. Affect flat, answers brief but coherent today.

PHQ-9: 16.

A/P:
1. Schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, per psychiatry. Agree with plan. Encouraged her to keep therapy weekly and to keep the medication conversation open with psychiatry. Safety plan reviewed, crisis line in her phone.
2. Weight: small meals and a protein drink if she isn't eating; recheck at next visit.
Physical still owed; will fold it in next time. RTC 3 months or sooner.

documents.author: psychiatry

OUTSIDE PSYCHIATRY GROUP
Follow-up visit, 8/23/2022
Re: Paige Howland

Seen three months after her initial evaluation. The main concern today is new to us: for about half a year she has been preoccupied with her nose, which she believes is grotesquely oversized and misshapen. She spends several hours a day examining it in mirrors and applies heavy makeup to hide it. No injury to the nose, no prior nasal surgery.

She continues weekly therapy. Psychotic symptoms present at a lower level; mood remains low. No suicidal intent or plan.

Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: unchanged (maternal depression, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia in maternal relatives).
Social: graduate student, never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: nose of normal size and shape, no deformity. Breathing comfortably. Remainder of the exam normal.

Assessment:
1. Body dysmorphic disorder, new.
2. Schizoaffective disorder, depressive type.

Plan: She asked for a referral to a plastic surgeon for rhinoplasty. I explained that cosmetic surgery does not relieve body dysmorphic disorder and often leaves people more distressed, so I am not making that referral. Recommended her therapist address the appearance concerns directly. Raised medication again; she will think about it. Return in about 8 weeks.

Copy to primary care.

documents.title: Referral question
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi, could you send a referral to a plastic surgeon? My psychiatrist won't do it. It's about my nose. I've thought about it a lot and it's what I want.

documents.title: RE: Referral question
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Paige, thanks for asking me directly. I read your psychiatrist's letter, and I agree with them, so I'm not going to send that referral. Surgery doesn't usually take this kind of worry away, and it can make it worse. I know how much this weighs on you. Can you bring it to your therapist this week? I'm also glad to talk it over at your next visit.

REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Visit 5/28/2025, 16:45
Patient: Paige Howland, 29F

CC: brought by roommate for suicidal statements.

HPI: Roommate tells us that over the past month the patient has repeatedly talked about wanting to "end it all," has stopped going to her therapy appointments, and has been saving up her pills. Patient has schizoaffective disorder and body dysmorphic disorder and has been on sertraline for several years, previously stable. She tells me she has been isolating more and more this month and feels hopeless. She admits to collecting her medication. Denies taking any of it or any other act toward suicide today, but repeats that life is not worth living.

PMH: schizoaffective disorder, depressive type; body dysmorphic disorder; prior major depressive episodes. PSH: none.
Meds: sertraline 50 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.
Family: mother depression, maternal aunt bipolar, maternal uncle schizophrenia.
Social: graduate student, lives with roommate. Never smoker, no alcohol, no drugs.

Vitals stable throughout.
Exam: unkempt, avoids eye contact, speaks quietly in a flat monotone. Otherwise normal exam: heart regular, lungs clear, abdomen soft, no signs of ingestion or injury.

Labs: Na 140, K 4.1, Cl 102, HCO3 24, BUN 18, Cr 0.9, glucose 98. TSH 2.5. Urine drug screen negative.

MDM: medically clear. Active suicidal ideation with means gathered. Emergency psychiatry consulted; she agreed to voluntary admission.

Disposition: admitted to inpatient psychiatry.
Copy to PCP.

Legal status: voluntary

Admitting diagnosis: suicidal ideation in the setting of schizoaffective disorder, depressive type.
Other: body dysmorphic disorder.

Course: Admitted from the ED after the roommate reported suicidal talk and stockpiled medication. On the unit she was withdrawn for the first two days, then engaged in groups and individual sessions. documents.author: psychiatry

INPATIENT PSYCHIATRIC UNIT, REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER
Admitted 5/22/2026, discharged 6/4/2026
Patient: Paige Howland

Principal diagnosis: suicidal ideation; schizoaffective disorder, depressive type.
Other: body dysmorphic disorder.

Course: Admitted from the ED after her roommate found her on the roof edge. Second admission for suicidal ideation in a year. For the first several days she was guarded and slept little. Given recurrent depressive episodes with psychosis, an antipsychotic was recommended; she agreed, and paliperidone ER 6 mg each morning was started, with sertraline 50 mg daily continued. She tolerated it without stiffness, restlessness or dizziness. Appetite and sleep gradually improved. No self-harm on the unit. By discharge she denied suicidal intent, could name reasons for living and her supports, and had updated her safety plan with her roommate and parents.

Discharge medications:
- paliperidone ER 6 mg by mouth every morning (new)
- sertraline 50 mg by mouth daily (unchanged)
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: outpatient psychiatry and therapy within one week (booked); primary care within 2 weeks. PCP asked to follow weight and metabolic labs on the new antipsychotic.

documents.body:
Seen after her second psychiatric admission. ED record and discharge summary reviewed.

She says this spring "crept up": stopped eating much, slept 3-4 hours, stopped texting friends. Glad her roommate found her. On the unit she started paliperidone 6 mg each morning and stays on sertraline 50. She has seen psychiatry (6/10) and her therapist twice since discharge.

Side effects: a little sleepy in the mornings, no stiffness or restlessness. Eating more again.

Safety: denies current suicidal thoughts or plan. Parents have the medications and hand her a week at a time. No firearms.

Exam: thin, appropriately dressed, fair eye contact, speech slow but organized. Weight 56.4, up a little from the ED (55.6), still about 5 kg under her usual 61. BP and pulse normal. Heart and lungs normal. No tremor, no rigidity.

PHQ-9: 12.

Meds: paliperidone ER 6 mg every morning (psychiatry, new), sertraline 50 mg daily (psychiatry). NKDA.

A/P:
1. Suicidal ideation, recent admission: safety plan reviewed and updated; it's on her phone and the fridge. Psychiatry and therapy weekly.
2. Schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, now on paliperidone: baseline A1c and fasting lipids today for antipsychotic monitoring; I'll follow weight here.
3. Weight loss from the depressive episode: regular meals, add snacks. Recheck at next visit.
4. BDD: unchanged, therapy.
RTC in 3 months, sooner for anything. Nurse will check in by phone.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Paige, your A1c (blood sugar average) and cholesterol are both normal. These are a starting point now that you're on paliperidone; we'll repeat them in a few months.

documents.title: RE: Lab results
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Thanks. Feeling a little more like a person this week.

documents.title: Nurse check-in
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Check-in call. Pt says mood slowly better, sleeping 7 hours, eating three meals. Taking both meds; morning grogginess less. No thoughts of self-harm. Therapy weekly. No needs for PCP right now.

documents.title: Psychiatry Follow-up
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
OUTSIDE PSYCHIATRY GROUP
Follow-up, 7/14/2026
Re: Paige Howland

Six weeks after discharge. Mood slowly improving. Sleep and appetite better. No hallucinations. No suicidal thoughts. Engaged in weekly therapy; parents remain involved.

Medications: paliperidone ER 6 mg every morning, sertraline 50 mg daily. Mild morning sedation, fading. No extrapyramidal signs on exam.

Plan: continue both at current doses. Return in 4 weeks.

cc: PCP
